theories.name: K3 sigma models
aliases: Worldsheet theory of type II strings on K3
theories.summary: The $\mathcal{N}=(4,4)$ superconformal sigma models with a K3 surface as target, $c = 6$: an 80-dimensional moduli space, elliptic genus $2\phi_{0,1}$ with Mathieu moonshine, and symmetry groups inside Conway's group. Fermionic theories.
theories.description:
The supersymmetric sigma model on a K3 surface with a Ricci-flat metric and a $B$-field is conformal. Because the metric is hyperkähler, its superconformal symmetry is $\mathcal{N}=(4,4)$ with $c = 6$: the $\mathcal{N}=(2,2)$ algebra extended by an $su(2)\oplus su(2)$ current algebra at level 1 [@k3-sigma-models/nw2001]. These are fermionic theories, with Neveu–Schwarz and Ramond sectors. The $\mathcal{N}=(4,4)$ theories with $c = 6$ form two components, associated with $T^4$ (16-dimensional) and with K3 (80-dimensional) [@k3-sigma-models/nw2001].

**Moduli space.** Its real dimension is 80: 40 for complex structures, 20 for Kähler forms and 22 for the $B$-field, minus 2 because each Ricci-flat metric has a sphere of complex structures [@k3-sigma-models/am1996, fn. 1]. Aspinwall and Morrison [@k3-sigma-models/am1996, Eq. (14)] determined the global form
$$\mathcal{M}_{\rm K3} = O(\Gamma^{4,20})\backslash O(4,20)/(O(4)\times O(20)).$$
A point is a positive-definite four-plane $\Pi\subset\mathbb{R}^{4,20}\cong H^{\rm even}(\mathrm{K3},\mathbb{R})$, and $\Gamma^{4,20}$ is the even unimodular lattice $H^{\rm even}(\mathrm{K3},\mathbb{Z})$ of D-brane charges [@k3-sigma-models/ghv2012] (GHV: Gaberdiel, Hohenegger and Volpato). Nahm and Wendland [@k3-sigma-models/nw2001] treat worldsheet parity as a symmetry rather than an identification and write the moduli space with $O^+(H^{\rm even}(\mathrm{K3},\mathbb{Z}))$ acting on $O^+(4,20)/(SO(4)\times O(20))$. The theory is expected to be singular where $\Pi$ is orthogonal to a vector of norm $-2$ [@k3-sigma-models/ghv2012].

**Elliptic genus.** The elliptic genus $\mathrm{Tr}_{\rm RR}(-1)^{F_L+F_R}q^{L_0-\frac{c}{24}}\bar q^{\bar L_0-\frac{c}{24}}e^{4\pi izJ^3_0}$, with $\frac{c}{24} = \frac14$, is the same at every point of the moduli space, because the weak Jacobi forms of weight 0 and index 1 form a one-dimensional space [@k3-sigma-models/eot2011; @k3-sigma-models/gannon2016] (EOT: Eguchi, Ooguri and Tachikawa):
$$\phi_{\rm K3}(\tau,z) = 8\sum_{i=2}^{4}\frac{\theta_i(\tau,z)^2}{\theta_i(\tau,0)^2} = 2\phi_{0,1}(\tau,z) = 2y + 20 + 2y^{-1} + O(q),\qquad y = e^{2\pi iz}.$$
At $z = 0$ it is the Euler number 24 of K3, and at $z = \frac12$ it is $16 + O(q)$, the signature [@k3-sigma-models/eot2011]. The 24 Ramond ground states have $h = \bar h = \frac14$ and split as $(\mathbf2,\mathbf2) + 20$ singlets under $SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_R$ [@k3-sigma-models/ghv2012].

### Mathieu moonshine
In terms of $\mathcal{N}=4$ characters [@k3-sigma-models/eot2011, Eq. (1.11)],
$$\phi_{\rm K3} = 20\,\mathrm{ch}_{\frac14,0} - 2\,\mathrm{ch}_{\frac14,\frac12} + 2\sum_{n\geq1}A_n\,q^{n-\frac18}\,\frac{\theta_1(\tau,z)^2}{\eta(\tau)^3},$$
with $A_n = 45, 231, 770, 2277, 5796, 13915, 30843, \dots$. EOT [@k3-sigma-models/eot2011] observed that $A_1,\dots,A_5$ are dimensions of irreducible representations of the Mathieu group $M_{24}$, and $A_6$, $A_7$ sums of such dimensions. Twined elliptic genera were then proposed for every element of $M_{24}$, and Gannon [@k3-sigma-models/gannon2016] proved that the resulting multiplicities are those of true $M_{24}$ representations. By the theorem below, the symmetry groups of individual K3 sigma models are not all subgroups of $M_{24}$, so the explanation of this $M_{24}$ structure must be more subtle [@k3-sigma-models/ghv2012].

### Symmetries and Conway's group
GHV [@k3-sigma-models/ghv2012] classified the symmetries that preserve the $\mathcal{N}=(4,4)$ algebra and the spectral flow operators. At any non-singular point they form a subgroup of $\mathrm{Co}_0 = \mathrm{Aut}(\Lambda)$, the automorphism group of the Leech lattice, that fixes pointwise a sublattice of $\Lambda$ of rank at least 4; it does not contain $-1$, so it is also a subgroup of $\mathrm{Co}_1$. This is the stringy analogue of the Mukai–Kondo theorem, which puts the symplectic automorphisms of a K3 surface in $M_{23}$. The theorem allows four cases, one of which is a subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}_2^{11}$ extended by a subgroup of $M_{24}$ with at least four orbits; the other three are not subgroups of $M_{24}$.

### Special loci and rational points
- **$T^4/\mathbb{Z}_2$ orbifolds.** The $\mathbb{Z}_2$ orbifold embeds the 16-dimensional moduli space of torus theories in $\mathcal{M}_{\rm K3}$, with $B$-field $\frac12$ on the exceptional divisors [@k3-sigma-models/nw2001]. The torus moduli vary continuously along it, so the theory is rational only at special points (for tori, see [@k3-sigma-models/gv2004]). GHV [@k3-sigma-models/ghv2012] find symmetries outside $M_{24}$ already at the orbifold of the self-dual torus.
- **Gepner model $(2)^4$.** Rational. Nahm and Wendland [@k3-sigma-models/nw2001, Sec. 3] prove that it is the $\mathbb{Z}_4$ orbifold of the torus theory with lattice $\mathbb{Z}^4$ and has a geometric interpretation on the Fermat quartic, and that the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_4$ orbifold loci do not meet there, contrary to an earlier conjecture.
- **Gepner model $(1)^6$.** Rational, with symmetry group $\mathbb{Z}_3^4\rtimes A_6$, not a subgroup of $M_{24}$ [@k3-sigma-models/ghv2012].
- **The $\mathbb{Z}_2^8:\mathbb{M}_{20}$ model.** The $\mathbb{Z}_2$ orbifold of the $D_4$-torus theory, whose bosonic part has $so(8)_1$ currents on each side, i.e. the sigma model on the tetrahedral Kummer surface. It is also a theory of twelve free Majorana fermions on each side, a rational theory based on $su(2)_1^{\oplus 6}$, and a $\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2$ orbifold of the Gepner model $(2)^4$. Its symmetry group $\mathbb{Z}_2^8:\mathbb{M}_{20}$ is one of the largest maximal symmetry groups of K3 sigma models [@k3-sigma-models/gtvw2014].

theories.name: Symmetric orbifold CFTs
aliases: D1–D5 CFT at the orbifold point
theories.summary: The orbifold $X^{\otimes N}/S_N$ of $N$ copies of a seed CFT $X$, with $c = N c_X$. Its spectrum follows from that of $X$ [@symmetric-orbifold/dmvv1997] and is universal at large $N$; $\mathrm{Sym}^N(T^4)$ and $\mathrm{Sym}^N(\mathrm{K3})$ are believed to lie on the moduli spaces of the D1–D5 CFTs dual to $AdS_3$.
theories.description:
$\mathrm{Sym}^N(X)$ is the tensor product of $N$ copies of a seed CFT $X$, orbifolded by the symmetric group $S_N$ that permutes them, so $c = N c_X$. Its Hilbert space is a sum of twisted sectors labelled by conjugacy classes of $S_N$, i.e. by cycle types $(1)^{N_1}(2)^{N_2}\cdots$ with $\sum_n nN_n = N$; each sector keeps the states invariant under the centralizer $\prod_n S_{N_n}\ltimes\mathbb{Z}_n^{N_n}$ [@symmetric-orbifold/dmvv1997, Eqs. (2.1)–(2.4)] (DMVV: Dijkgraaf, Moore, Verlinde and Verlinde). A cycle of length $n$ joins $n$ copies of $X$ into one copy on an $n$ times longer circle, a "long string". For a bosonic seed with a unique vacuum, the lightest state of the $n$-cycle sector has $h = \bar h = \frac{c_X}{24}(n - \frac1n)$ (derived). If $X$ is fermionic, as for $T^4$ and K3, so is $\mathrm{Sym}^N(X)$. The members listed below take a seed with $c_X = 6$, $X = T^4$ or K3.

**Generating functions.** If the elliptic genus of $X$ is $\chi(X;q,y) = \sum_{m,\ell}c(m,\ell)\,q^my^\ell$, then [@symmetric-orbifold/dmvv1997, Eq. (1.3)]
$$\sum_{N\geq0}p^N\chi(\mathrm{Sym}^NX;q,y) = \prod_{n>0,\,m\geq0,\,\ell}\frac{1}{(1-p^nq^my^\ell)^{c(nm,\ell)}}.$$
The right side is the partition function of a second-quantized string on $X\times S^1$, and the generating function is (almost) an automorphic form for $O(3,2;\mathbb{Z})$ [@symmetric-orbifold/dmvv1997]. For $X = $ K3 at $y = 1$ it reduces to $\prod_{n}(1-p^n)^{-24}$, the generating function of orbifold Euler numbers (derived). For a bosonic seed (all states of integer spin) the torus partition functions obey an analogous product formula [@symmetric-orbifold/keller2011, Eq. (2.3); @symmetric-orbifold/hks2014, Eq. (5.4)] (HKS: Hartman, Keller and Stoica); it does not apply as written to fermionic seeds such as $T^4$ and K3, whose half-integer-spin states it would remove already at $N = 1$, so for those only the elliptic-genus formula above is quoted.

### Universality at large N
As $N\to\infty$ the free energy per copy becomes universal, depending only on $c_X$, with a first-order phase transition at $\beta = 2\pi$, the analogue of the Hawking–Page transition. The number of states grows as $e^{4\pi\sqrt{m\bar m}}$ [@symmetric-orbifold/keller2011]. HKS [@symmetric-orbifold/hks2014] show that every 2d CFT with large $c$ and a sparse light spectrum, $\rho(E)\lesssim e^{2\pi(E + c/12)}$ for light states with $E = \Delta - \frac{c}{12}$ below a small positive cutoff, has a universal free energy and Cardy growth for $\Delta \geq \frac{c}{6}$. Symmetric orbifolds satisfy this, and their light spectrum saturates the bound,
$$S(E) \simeq \frac{\pi c}{6} + 2\pi E,\qquad 0 < E < \frac{c}{12},$$
so in this sense they have the densest spectrum compatible with 3d gravity [@symmetric-orbifold/hks2014].

### D1–D5 system and AdS$_3$
The D1–D5 system on $X = T^4$ or K3 has near-horizon geometry $AdS_3\times S^3\times X$. For $X = T^4$ with $Q_1$ D1-branes and $Q_5$ D5-branes its boundary CFT has $c = 6Q_1Q_5$ [@symmetric-orbifold/sw1999]. For $X = $ K3 with coprime $Q_1, Q_5 > 0$, the Mukai vector $v = (Q_5, 0, -Q_1)$ is primitive with $v\cdot v = 2Q_1Q_5$, and the moduli space of stable sheaves is smooth and deformation equivalent to the Hilbert scheme $\mathrm{K3}^{[Q_1Q_5+1]}$, whose orbifold limit is $\mathrm{Sym}^{Q_1Q_5+1}(\mathrm{K3})$; so $N = Q_1Q_5 + 1$ and $c = 6(Q_1Q_5+1)$ in this charge convention ([@symmetric-orbifold/dijkgraaf1999, Sec. 5.1, Eqs. (3.8), (5.1), (7.7)]; the shift is subleading at large charge). Non-primitive charges need separate treatment [@symmetric-orbifold/dijkgraaf1999]. The CFT is believed to lie on the moduli space of $\mathrm{Sym}^N(X)$ with this $N$, but it is not known where on that moduli space, if anywhere, the orbifold point sits; at the loci where the branes can separate the CFT is singular [@symmetric-orbifold/sw1999]. The orbifold point is a weak-coupling limit without a good geometric description [@symmetric-orbifold/hks2014]. For $N \geq 2$ the moduli space of $\mathrm{Sym}^N(T^4)$ has 20 parameters (the 16 torus moduli plus 4 from the twist-2 sector), and generic twisted-sector deformations away from the orbifold point make the theory interacting; $N = 1$ is the free $T^4$ theory with 16 moduli [@symmetric-orbifold/egg2019] (EGG: Eberhardt, Gaberdiel and Gopakumar).

EGG [@symmetric-orbifold/egg2019] proposed a worldsheet dual of the large-$N$ orbifold point. Superstring theory on $AdS_3\times S^3\times T^4$ with one unit of NS–NS flux ($k = 1$), defined in the hybrid formalism with a $\mathfrak{psu}(1,1|2)_1$ WZW model, has no long-string continuum. Its spectrum matches the large-$N$ limit of $\mathrm{Sym}^N(T^4)$, and the worldsheet reproduces the fusion rules of the orbifold ([@symmetric-orbifold/egg2019], following [@symmetric-orbifold/gg2018]).

theories.name: Cigar CFT ($SL(2,\mathbb{R})/U(1)$)
theories.summary: The coset $SL(2,\mathbb{R})_k/U(1)$: a sigma model on a semi-infinite cigar with a dilaton, Witten's 2d Euclidean black hole, with $c=\frac{3k}{k-2}-1$. It is dual to sine-Liouville theory (FZZ), and its $\mathcal{N}=2$ version is mirror to $\mathcal{N}=2$ Liouville theory.
theories.description:
Witten [@cigar-cft/witten1991] found an exact CFT for a black hole in two-dimensional spacetime, the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})/U(1)$ gauged WZW
model at level $k$. Its Euclidean version is the cigar CFT, the coset $SL(2,\mathbb{R})_k/U(1)$, which can also be
written as $H_3^+/U(1)$ [@cigar-cft/kkk2002]. Gawedzki [@cigar-cft/gawedzki1991] constructed it by gauging a one-parameter group of
boosts in the $H_3^+$ model, which makes the Euclidean theory manifestly stable. The coset is defined for all $k>2$.
For large $k$ it is the sigma model with metric and dilaton
$$ds^2=k\,(d\rho^2+\tanh^2\rho\,d\varphi^2),\qquad\Phi=\Phi_0-\log\cosh\rho,\qquad\varphi\sim\varphi+2\pi,$$
in units $\alpha'=1$, with string coupling $e^\Phi$ [@cigar-cft/gr2015, Eqs. (1)–(2)] (Hori and Kapustin [@cigar-cft/hk2001] and Kazakov, Kostov and Kutasov [@cigar-cft/kkk2002] write $\Phi_0-2\log\cosh\rho$, a different normalization of the dilaton). The asymptotic slope then gives $c \approx 2 + \frac6k$ at large $k$, consistent with the exact $c$ below. The circle shrinks at the tip $\rho=0$, where the string coupling $e^\Phi$ is largest, so the
target is a semi-infinite cigar. As $\rho\to\infty$ it becomes a cylinder of radius $\sqrt k$ with a linear dilaton,
$\Phi\sim-\rho$, and $e^\Phi\to0$ [@cigar-cft/hk2001]. The exact background charge of the linear dilaton is
$Q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{k-2}}$ [@cigar-cft/hs2009], and a compact boson plus a linear dilaton with this $Q$ has
$c=1+(1+6Q^2)=\frac{2(k+1)}{k-2}$.

The central charge is $c=\frac{3k}{k-2}-1$, that of $SL(2,\mathbb{R})_k$ minus one for the gauged $U(1)$. It tends
to 2 as $k\to\infty$, where the cigar is weakly curved, and equals 26 at $k=\frac94$, where the cigar is a solution
of two-dimensional bosonic string theory [@cigar-cft/witten1991].

Vertex operators carry a radial label $j$, a momentum $n$ and a winding $w$ around the cigar. Momentum is conserved,
but winding is not, because a wound string can slip off the tip [@cigar-cft/kkk2002]. Hanany, Prezas and
Troost [@cigar-cft/hpt2002] computed the torus partition function from the path integral and found the spectrum expected from the coset
construction. With the Casimir written as $-j(j-1)$, as on the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ WZW page, it has a continuum
$j=\frac12+is$, $s\in\mathbb{R}$, with
$$h=\frac{s^2+\frac14}{k-2}+\frac{(n-kw)^2}{4k},\qquad\bar h=\frac{s^2+\frac14}{k-2}+\frac{(n+kw)^2}{4k},$$
and discrete states with $h=-\frac{j(j-1)}{k-2}+\frac{(n-kw)^2}{4k}$ and $\bar h$ the same with $n+kw$. For the
discrete states the constraint $J^3_0+\bar J^3_0=-kw$ fixes $j$, which lies in $\frac12<j<\frac{k-1}{2}$, the bound
of the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ model. Earlier, Dijkgraaf, Verlinde and Verlinde [@cigar-cft/dvv1992] studied the spectrum, the winding states
and the bound states of the Euclidean solution, and found that in the Lorentzian black hole target-space duality
exchanges the horizon and the singularity.

### FZZ duality
Fateev, Zamolodchikov and Zamolodchikov conjectured, in unpublished work presented by Kazakov, Kostov and Kutasov [@cigar-cft/kkk2002],
that the cigar CFT is equivalent to sine-Liouville theory, a compact boson $x$ and a linear dilaton $\phi$ with a
winding-mode potential,
$$\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{4\pi}\Big[(\partial x)^2+(\partial\phi)^2+Q\hat R\phi+\lambda\,e^{b\phi}\cos R(x_L-x_R)\Big],\qquad Q^2=\frac{1}{k-2},\quad R=\sqrt k,\quad b=-\frac1Q .$$
Its central charge $2+6Q^2$ equals that of the cigar, and $b$ makes the potential marginal. The duality is
strong–weak: the cigar is weakly coupled at large $k$, sine-Liouville theory as $k\to2$. In one description the
strong-coupling end of the asymptotic cylinder is capped off by the tip of the cigar, in the other it is cut off by
the potential, which also breaks winding conservation. Two- and three-point functions agree. Hikida and Schomerus [@cigar-cft/hs2009]
proved that all correlators of tachyon vertex operators agree, on the sphere and on all closed surfaces, by
combining the $H_3^+$–Liouville correspondence with the self-duality of Liouville theory.

### The supersymmetric cigar
The $\mathcal{N}=2$ version is the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})_k/U(1)$ Kazama–Suzuki supercoset, the fermionic 2d black hole:
an $\mathcal{N}=(2,2)$ SCFT with $c=3\big(1+\frac2k\big)$, defined for all $k>0$. Unlike in the bosonic case, the
$1/k$ expansion of its central charge stops at one loop. Hori and Kapustin [@cigar-cft/hk2001] proved that it is equivalent to
$\mathcal{N}=2$ Liouville theory and that this equivalence is mirror symmetry, by realizing the supercoset as the
infrared limit of a gauged linear sigma model and dualizing. The lowest weight in its spectrum is
$h_{\min}=\frac{1}{4k}$, so the effective central charge is $c-24h_{\min}=3$.

### Status
Gawedzki [@cigar-cft/gawedzki1991, Sec. 5] expected the Euclidean black hole CFT to be unitary, citing the result of Dixon, Lykken and Peskin [@cigar-cft/dlp1989] that the
conditions $J^3_n|\psi\rangle=0$, $n\geq1$, remove the negative-norm states of the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ modules for
discrete spins in a range bounded by $\frac{k}{2}$.

The cigar is also the coset $H_3^+/U(1)$ [@cigar-cft/gawedzki1991; @cigar-cft/kkk2002]. Hikida and Schomerus [@cigar-cft/hs2009] obtain its correlators from those of the $H_3^+$ model, and through them from Liouville theory.

theories.name: Conway moonshine module
theories.summary: The unique self-dual holomorphic $\mathcal{N}=1$ super vertex operator algebra with $c = 12$ and no weight-$\tfrac12$ fields: a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ orbifold of 24 free chiral fermions. A fermionic theory whose symmetries realize moonshine for Conway's group.
theories.description:
This is a fermionic theory: a self-dual (holomorphic) super vertex operator algebra (SVOA), with
states of half-integer weight, $c_L = 12$ and $c_R = 0$. Duncan and Mack-Crane [@conway-module/dmc2015] proved that it is
the unique $C_2$-cofinite rational SVOA of CFT type that has central charge 12, is self-dual, and
has no non-zero states of weight $\tfrac12$. Duncan [@conway-module/duncan2007] proved the analogous characterization among
$\mathcal{N}=1$ SVOAs. This is the super analogue of the (open) FLM characterization of the Monster
CFT by $c = 24$, self-duality and no weight-1 states.

**Constructions.** (i) Frenkel, Lepowsky and Meurman [@conway-module/flm1985, Sec. 15] first described it as a $\mathbb{Z}_2$
orbifold of the SVOA of 8 free fermions and 8 chiral bosons on the $E_8$ lattice, by a lift of $-1$; this removes the
8 weight-$\tfrac12$ fermions. (ii) Duncan [@conway-module/duncan2007] built the same space from 24 free chiral fermions, using the
Golay code, and showed it is isomorphic to (i). (iii) Duncan and Mack-Crane [@conway-module/dmc2015] realize $V^{s\natural}$ as
a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ orbifold of the Clifford module SVOA of a 24-dimensional space (24 free fermions); its
even part is the lattice vertex operator algebra of type $D_{12}$. It has a unique canonically twisted
(Ramond) module.

**Character.** In the Neveu–Schwarz sector,
$$\mathrm{tr}\,q^{L_0 - \frac12} = \frac{\theta_{E_8}(\tau)\,\eta(\tau)^8}{\eta(\tau/2)^8\,\eta(2\tau)^8} - 8
= q^{-1/2}\prod_{n\geq1}(1+q^{n-1/2})^{24} - 24
= q^{-1/2} + 276\,q^{1/2} + 2048\,q + 11202\,q^{3/2} + 49152\,q^2 + \dots$$
(Duncan [@conway-module/duncan2007, Eq. (1.0.2)]; Witten [@conway-module/witten2007, Eqs. (3.34)–(3.36)], where it is the function $K$). The middle form, 24
free fermions minus their 24 weight-$\tfrac12$ states, is derived and agrees with both. The 276 weight-1
states span $\mathfrak{so}(24)$ ($276 = \dim\mathfrak{so}(24)$, derived), and the weight-$\tfrac32$ space is
a half-spin module of $\mathrm{Spin}_{24}(\mathbb{R})$ (dimension $2^{11} = 2048$).

**Supersymmetry and symmetry.** An $\mathcal{N}=1$ supercurrent is a weight-$\tfrac32$ vector, i.e. a
spinor of $\mathrm{Spin}(24)$, satisfying quadratic conditions; Duncan [@conway-module/duncan2007] showed such vectors form a
single orbit, so the $\mathcal{N}=1$ structure is unique. Fixing it breaks the continuous symmetry to a
finite group: the automorphism group of the $\mathcal{N}=1$ SVOA is $\mathrm{Co}_1$, Conway's largest
sporadic group [@conway-module/duncan2007]. Duncan and Mack-Crane [@conway-module/dmc2015] instead use a faithful action of
$\mathrm{Co}_0 = \mathrm{Aut}(\Lambda)$, the automorphism group of the Leech lattice, a double cover of
$\mathrm{Co}_1 = \mathrm{Co}_0/\{\pm1\}$; Witten [@conway-module/witten2007] describes the symmetry of the SCFT as $\mathrm{Co}_0$.

**Moonshine and K3.** For every $g \in \mathrm{Co}_0$ the graded supertrace $T^s_g$ on $V^{s\natural}$ is
the normalized principal modulus of a genus-zero group, the analogue of monstrous moonshine
[@conway-module/dmc2015]. It is related to the principal moduli $t_g$ that Conway and Norton [@conway-module/conwaynorton1979] and Queen [@conway-module/queen1981] attached to
$\mathrm{Co}_0$ by $T^s_g(2\tau) = t_g(\tau) + \chi_g$, with $\chi_g$ the trace of $g$ on $\Lambda\otimes\mathbb{C}$.
The canonically twisted module attaches a weak Jacobi form of weight 0 and index 1 to each symplectic derived autoequivalence of a K3 surface fixing a
stability condition. These recover the twined elliptic genera of K3 sigma models in all available
examples, the identity giving the K3 elliptic genus. The supersymmetry-preserving symmetry groups of K3
sigma models lie in Conway's group [@conway-module/ghv2012].

symmetry.spacetime: One $\mathcal{N}=1$ super-Virasoro algebra at $c = 12$, on the holomorphic side only ($\bar c = 0$) — 2d conformal symmetry, no parity (holomorphic); $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal on one side (1 $Q$ + 1 $S$ supercharge)

theories.name: $H_3^+$ WZW model
aliases: Sigma model on hyperbolic space $H_3$ with an NS–NS $B$-field
theories.summary: The WZW-type sigma model on Euclidean $AdS_3$, $H_3^+=SL(2,\mathbb{C})/SU(2)$, at real level $k>2$: $c=\frac{3k}{k-2}$, a continuum of primaries with $j\in-\frac12+i\mathbb{R}$, exact two- and three-point functions, and sphere correlators given by Liouville theory. Not unitary.
theories.description:
The $H_3^+$ model is the sigma model with a Wess–Zumino term whose target is three-dimensional hyperbolic space
$H_3^+=SL(2,\mathbb{C})/SU(2)$, the hermitian $2\times2$ matrices of determinant one, that is, Euclidean $AdS_3$
with an NS–NS $B$-field. It is obtained from the $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ WZW model by gauging $SU(2)$ [@h3-wzw/gawedzki1991]. The
chiral algebra is two commuting $\widehat{sl}(2)_k$ current algebras, and the Sugawara stress tensor has
$c=\frac{3k}{k-2}$. The level $k$ is real, and the Euclidean functional integral is stable for $k>2$. As
$k\to\infty$ the model reduces to quantum mechanics on $H_3^+$; as $k\to2$, the critical level, the
Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov equations reduce to the eigenvalue equations of the Gaudin Hamiltonians
[@h3-wzw/rt2005].

The primary fields $\Phi^j(x|z)$ carry a spin $j$ and a label $x\in\mathbb{C}$ for the $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ quantum
numbers (in string theory on $AdS_3$, a point on the boundary). With $b^2=\frac{1}{k-2}$ their weights are
$\Delta_j=\bar\Delta_j=-b^2j(j+1)=-\frac{j(j+1)}{k-2}$. The spectrum is the continuum
$j\in-\frac12+i\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}$, built on the principal series of $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ that decomposes
$L^2(H_3^+)$, and $\Phi^j$ is identified with $\Phi^{-j-1}$ by reflection [@h3-wzw/teschner1997, Sec. 3.1, Eq. (40)]. At $j=-\frac12+is$,
$\Delta_j=\frac{1/4+s^2}{k-2}>0$. The vacuum is not normalizable, like that of a free boson on $\mathbb{R}$, but it
lies $\frac{1}{4(k-2)}$ below the continuum, so it is not a limit of normalizable states; Gawedzki [@h3-wzw/gawedzki1991] showed that these
representations and their descendants make up the whole space of states [@h3-wzw/mo2002]. Unlike for compact
WZW models, the representations do not factorize into left and right current-algebra modules.

The model is not unitary [@h3-wzw/teschner1997, Sec. 1; @h3-wzw/gawedzki1991, Sec. 1]. On a Euclidean worldsheet the action is real and positive, because
the $B$-field is imaginary there, and normalizable operators have positive weights, so the Euclidean theory is well
behaved. But the hermitian form that makes the Hamiltonian symmetric is not positive definite [@h3-wzw/teschner1997, Sec. 2.1; @h3-wzw/teschner1999, Sec. 2.1], and on a
Lorentzian worldsheet the action is complex and the modes $J^3_{-n}$ create negative-norm states
[@h3-wzw/mo2002]. The model is used as the Euclidean version of the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ WZW model for strings on $AdS_3$, and
as the parent of the Euclidean black hole coset $H_3^+/U(1)$.

### Correlation functions
Teschner [@h3-wzw/teschner1997] derived the structure constants from crossing symmetry of four-point functions with a degenerate field, the
method that gives the DOZZ formula in Liouville theory, and the reflection amplitude from them. He then established
the operator product expansion and the factorization of four-point functions [@h3-wzw/teschner1999], and proved crossing
symmetry by reduction to Liouville theory [@h3-wzw/teschner2001]. In the basis $\Phi^j(\mu|z)=\frac{1}{\pi}|\mu|^{2j+2}\int d^2x\,e^{\mu x-\bar\mu\bar
x}\,\Phi^j(x|z)$ of Ribault and Teschner [@h3-wzw/rt2005],
$$\langle\Phi^{j_2}(\mu_2|z_2)\Phi^{j_1}(\mu_1|z_1)\rangle=|z_{21}|^{-4\Delta_{j_1}}|\mu_1|^2\,\delta^{(2)}(\mu_2+\mu_1)\big(\delta(j_2+j_1+1)+R^H(j_1)\,\delta(j_2-j_1)\big).$$
The three-point function is $\delta^{(2)}(\mu_1+\mu_2+\mu_3)$ times an $SL(2,\mathbb{C})$ Clebsch–Gordan
coefficient, the usual powers of $|z_{ij}|$, and the structure constant $C^H(j_3,j_2,j_1)$. The table above gives
$R^H$ and $C^H$, with $\gamma(x)=\Gamma(x)/\Gamma(1-x)$, $j^r_{st}=j_s+j_t-j_r$, and
$\Upsilon_b(x)=1/\big(\Gamma_b(x)\Gamma_b(Q-x)\big)$, $Q=b+b^{-1}$, the function of the DOZZ formula defined on the
Liouville CFT page; it obeys $\Upsilon_b(x+b)=\gamma(bx)\,b^{1-2bx}\,\Upsilon_b(x)$ and $\Upsilon_b(\frac{Q}{2})=1$.

Ribault and Teschner [@h3-wzw/rt2005] proved that every $n$-point function on the sphere is a Liouville correlator with $n-2$ extra
degenerate fields:
$$\Big\langle\prod_{i=1}^n\Phi^{j_i}(\mu_i|z_i)\Big\rangle=\frac{\pi}{2}(-\pi)^{-n}b\,\delta^{(2)}\Big(\sum_i\mu_i\Big)|\Theta_n|^2\Big\langle\prod_{i=1}^nV_{\alpha_i}(z_i)\prod_{a=1}^{n-2}V_{-\frac{1}{2b}}(y_a)\Big\rangle .$$
The Liouville theory, in the conventions of Zamolodchikov and Zamolodchikov [@h3-wzw/zz1996], has the same $b$ and cosmological
constant $\mu_L=\frac{b^2}{\pi^2}$; the momenta are $\alpha_i=b(j_i+1)+\frac{1}{2b}$; the $y_a$ and $u$ are fixed by
$\sum_i\frac{\mu_i}{t-z_i}=u\,\frac{\prod_a(t-y_a)}{\prod_i(t-z_i)}$; and
$\Theta_n=u\prod_{r<s}z_{rs}^{1/2b^2}\prod_{a<a'}y_{aa'}^{1/2b^2}\prod_{r,a}(z_r-y_a)^{-1/2b^2}$. Then
$\Delta_j=\Delta_\alpha-\frac{k}{4}$ and $R^L(\alpha)=R^H(j)$. The proof relates the Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov and
Belavin–Polyakov–Zamolodchikov equations. Hikida and Schomerus [@h3-wzw/hs2009] derived the correspondence from the path integral and
extended it to higher genus.

parameters.description: Level of the $\widehat{sl}(2)_k$ current algebras, a real number; $b^2=\frac{1}{k-2}$. In the action [@h3-wzw/mo2002, Eq. The overall factor depends on the normalization of $d^2z$, which the source does not fix; Ribault and Teschner [@h3-wzw/rt2005] write $k$ in place of $\frac{k}{\pi}$.

theories.name: Holomorphic CFTs with $c = 24$
aliases: Holomorphic vertex operator algebras of central charge 24
theories.summary: Chiral CFTs with $c = 24$ and a single module, with $Z = J(\tau) + N$, $N = \dim V_1$. Schellekens [@holomorphic-c24/schellekens1993] found 71 possible weight-1 Lie algebras $V_1$; all 71 occur, and $V_1 \neq 0$ fixes the theory. Uniqueness for $V_1 = 0$ (the Monster CFT) is open.
theories.description:
A holomorphic (meromorphic, self-dual) CFT has only one irreducible module, the vacuum module.
Its character is invariant under $S$ and changes by a phase under $T$, so $c \in 8\mathbb{Z}$, and it is
a modular invariant partition function by itself when $c \in 24\mathbb{Z}$ [@holomorphic-c24/schellekens1993, Sec. 1].
For $c = 8$ and $16$ the only examples are the lattice theories of $E_8$, of $E_8\times E_8$, and of
$D_{16}$ with a spinor weight added. At $c = 24$, with $c_L = 24$ and $c_R = 0$, modular invariance fixes
$$Z(\tau) = J(\tau) + N = q^{-1} + N + 196884\,q + 21493760\,q^2 + \dots,\qquad N = \dim V_1,$$
so the theories differ already in their weight-1 currents [@holomorphic-c24/witten2007, Sec. 3.1].

**Schellekens' list.** The weight-1 currents form a Lie algebra $V_1$. Schellekens [@holomorphic-c24/schellekens1993, Sec. 2] showed, by
trace identities for the character twisted by the zero modes of the currents, that either $N = 0$,
or $N = 24$ and the theory is the Leech lattice CFT, or $N > 24$ and $V_1$ generates an affine
(current) algebra $\bigoplus_i (\mathfrak{g}_i)_{k_i}$ of total central charge 24 with
$$\frac{h^\vee_i}{k_i} = \frac{N - 24}{24}\quad\text{for every simple factor}.$$
This has 221 solutions; higher trace identities and modular invariance leave 69, each with exactly
one modular invariant combination of affine characters (up to outer automorphisms). With the Leech
lattice ($N = 24$) and $N = 0$ this gives 71 possible $V_1$. He assumed $N \neq 0$ for his methods, a finitely generated
chiral algebra, and one theory per character combination, and conjectured that all 71 exist. At
the time 41 were known: the 24 Niemeier lattice theories, 15 further theories from $\mathbb{Z}_2$
orbifolds $X \to -X$ of Niemeier theories (including the Monster CFT, from the Leech lattice), and
two more ($B_{8,1}E_{8,2}$ and $F_{4,6}A_{2,2}$). The list also classifies ten-dimensional heterotic
strings, through the embeddings of $D_{8,1}$.

**Status.** For strongly rational holomorphic vertex operator algebras of central charge 24:
(a) $V_1$ is $0$, 24-dimensional abelian, or one of the 69 semisimple Lie algebras of Schellekens [@holomorphic-c24/schellekens1993]
(van Ekeren, Möller and Scheithauer [@holomorphic-c24/ems2020] made Schellekens' argument a theorem; van Ekeren, Lam, Möller
and Shimakura [@holomorphic-c24/elms2021] gave a simpler proof); (b) every Lie algebra on the list is realized; (c) for
$V_1 \neq 0$, $V_1$ determines the theory up to isomorphism. Items (b) and (c) were proved case by
case by many authors, and Lam and Shimakura [@holomorphic-c24/ls2020] completed the uniqueness proof. Uniform proofs followed:
every theory with $V_1 \neq 0$ is a cyclic orbifold of the Leech lattice theory by a "generalised
deep hole" [@holomorphic-c24/ms2023], or of a Niemeier lattice theory (Höhn and Möller [@holomorphic-c24/hm2022], who also
prove uniqueness systematically); Betsumiya, Lam and Shimakura [@holomorphic-c24/bls2023] give another uniqueness proof. The
theories with $\mathrm{rank}\,V_1 = 24$ are exactly the Niemeier lattice theories. The remaining
open case is $V_1 = 0$: Frenkel, Lepowsky and Meurman [@holomorphic-c24/flm1988] conjectured that the Monster CFT is the only
such theory.

In Witten's proposal [@holomorphic-c24/witten2007] for three-dimensional gravity, the 70 theories with currents would be dual to
gravity coupled to Chern–Simons gauge fields, and the $V_1 = 0$ theory to pure gravity.

theories.name: Leech lattice CFT
aliases: 24 chiral bosons on the Leech lattice
theories.summary: The holomorphic $c = 24$ theory of 24 chiral bosons compactified on the Leech lattice $\Lambda$, with $Z = \Theta_\Lambda/\eta^{24} = J(\tau) + 24$. Since $\Lambda$ has no roots, its only weight-1 states are the 24 abelian currents $\partial X^i$.
theories.description:
For an even self-dual (unimodular) Euclidean lattice $L$ of rank $n$, the $n$ chiral bosons $X^i$
with momenta in $L$ form a holomorphic CFT with $c_L = n$, $c_R = 0$, whose character is
$\Theta_L(\tau)/\eta(\tau)^n$; it is modular invariant up to phases, and exactly invariant when
$n$ is a multiple of 24 [@leech-lattice-cft/schellekens1993, Sec. 1]. In rank 24 there are exactly 24 such lattices,
the Niemeier lattices, each fixed by its root system; the Leech lattice $\Lambda$ is the unique one
without roots, i.e. with no vectors of norm 2 [@leech-lattice-cft/conway1969]. Its shortest vectors have norm 4.

The vertex operators $e^{ip\cdot X}$, $p \in \Lambda$, have weight $h = p^2/2 \geq 2$, so the only
weight-1 states are the currents $\partial X^i$, generating $U(1)^{24}$. Modular invariance then
fixes the partition function to $J(\tau) + 24$:
$$Z(\tau) = \frac{\Theta_\Lambda(\tau)}{\eta(\tau)^{24}} = q^{-1} + 24 + 196884\,q + 21493760\,q^2 + \dots,
\qquad \Theta_\Lambda = E_4^3 - 720\,\Delta .$$
The theta series follows because $\Theta_\Lambda$ is a weight-12 modular form with no $q^1$ term
(derived; it gives 196560 vectors of norm 4). At weight 2 the $196884$ states are
$T$, the 24 descendants $\partial^2X^i$, and $196883 - 24 = 196859$ Virasoro primaries: the 196560
vertex operators of norm-4 momenta and the 299 traceless products $\partial X^i\partial X^j$ (derived).

Schellekens [@leech-lattice-cft/schellekens1993] showed that a holomorphic $c = 24$ theory whose weight-1 currents include an abelian
factor has exactly 24 currents, all abelian, and is the Leech lattice theory; it is No. 1 on his
list. Every holomorphic $c = 24$ theory with $V_1 \neq 0$ is a cyclic orbifold of this one
[@leech-lattice-cft/elms2021], and orbifolding by a lift of $X \to -X$ gives the
Monster CFT [@leech-lattice-cft/flm1988]. Conversely, the Leech lattice theory can itself be
obtained as an orbifold of another Niemeier lattice theory [@leech-lattice-cft/witten2007, Sec. 3.1].

Its automorphism group contains the inner automorphisms $\exp(a_{(0)})$, $a \in V_1$, generated
by the zero modes of the currents, and the outer automorphism group is
$\mathrm{Aut}(V_\Lambda)/\mathrm{Inn}(V_\Lambda) \cong O(\Lambda) = \mathrm{Co}_0$, Conway's group
[@leech-lattice-cft/bls2023, Remark 3.1, Table 1].

theories.name: Liouville CFT
theories.summary: The non-compact, non-rational CFT with only Virasoro symmetry and a diagonal continuum of scalar primaries above $h=\frac{c-1}{24}$. Its OPE data is the DOZZ formula, and it exists for every complex $c$ away from $(-\infty,1]$.
theories.description:
Liouville CFT solves the conformal bootstrap for every complex central charge
away from the half-line $c\leq 1$, with Virasoro as its only symmetry. It is
non-compact: the spectrum is a continuum of scalar primaries, and the identity
is not a normalisable operator. It is unitary when $c$ is real and $c>1$.

This page follows the conventions of Collier, Eberhardt, Mühlmann and
Rodriguez, *The Virasoro minimal string* [@liouville-cft/cemr2024]. The operators $V_P$ are reflection
symmetric, and the two- and three-point functions are the universal functions
$\rho_0^{(b)}$ and $C_b$.

$$c=1+6Q^2,\qquad Q=b+b^{-1},\qquad h_P=\bar h_P=\frac{Q^2}{4}+P^2=\frac{c-1}{24}+P^2.$$

The primaries $V_P$ are labelled by a Liouville momentum $P$, with $V_{-P}=V_P$.
The spectrum is the continuum $P\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$, in which each Verma
module $\mathcal{V}_P\otimes\overline{\mathcal{V}}_P$ appears once. In the
Lagrangian description $V_P\propto e^{2\alpha\phi}$ with
$\alpha=\frac{Q}{2}+iP$, so reflection is $\alpha\to Q-\alpha$. The parameter
$\mu$ only enters the normalisation of $e^{2\alpha\phi}$, so it does not appear
in $\rho_0^{(b)}$ or $C_b$.

There is significant evidence that Liouville CFT is the unique unitary CFT with
$c>1$ whose spectrum consists only of scalar Virasoro primaries, and more
generally of primaries of bounded spin.

### OPE measure and DOZZ formula

The OPE measure $\rho_0^{(b)}$ is the inverse of the two-point function:

$$\langle V_{P_1}(0)V_{P_2}(1)\rangle=\frac{1}{\rho_0^{(b)}(P_1)}\big(\delta(P_1-P_2)+\delta(P_1+P_2)\big),$$

$$\rho_0^{(b)}(P)=4\sqrt{2}\,\sinh(2\pi bP)\sinh(2\pi b^{-1}P)=\sqrt{2}\,\frac{\Gamma_b(Q\pm 2iP)}{\Gamma_b(\pm 2iP)}.$$

The three-point function is the DOZZ formula, written with the double gamma
function $\Gamma_b$ defined below:

$$\langle V_{P_1}(0)V_{P_2}(1)V_{P_3}(\infty)\rangle=C_b(P_1,P_2,P_3)=\frac{\Gamma_b(2Q)\,\Gamma_b(\frac{Q}{2}\pm iP_1\pm iP_2\pm iP_3)}{\sqrt{2}\,\Gamma_b(Q)^3\prod_{k=1}^{3}\Gamma_b(Q\pm 2iP_k)}.$$

Each $\pm$ denotes a product over both signs, so the numerator and the
denominator each contain nine factors of $\Gamma_b$. The function $C_b$ is
symmetric in its arguments and invariant under $P_j\to-P_j$ and $b\to b^{-1}$.

The identity is the continuation $P\to\frac{iQ}{2}$, and it reproduces the
two-point function. Near $P_1=P_2$,

$$C_b\big(P_1,P_2,\tfrac{iQ}{2}-i\varepsilon\big)\approx\frac{1}{\rho_0^{(b)}(P_1)}\,\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon^2+(P_1-P_2)^2}\xrightarrow{\;\varepsilon\to 0\;}\frac{\delta(P_1-P_2)}{\rho_0^{(b)}(P_1)}.$$

Both functions are universal, because they are crossing kernels of the identity.
$\rho_0^{(b)}$ is the modular kernel of the vacuum character. For a four-point
function of pairwise identical operators, the identity block in one channel is
$\int_0^\infty\mathrm{d}P\,\rho_0^{(b)}(P)\,C_b(P_1,P_2,P)$ times the blocks of
the cross channel. They therefore also govern the asymptotic data of unitary
compact 2d CFTs.

$C_b$ is fixed by crossing of a four-point function with a degenerate operator,
which gives the shift equation

$$\frac{C_b(P_1+ib,P_2,P_3)}{C_b(P_1,P_2,P_3)}=\frac{\Gamma(1+b^2-2ibP_1)\,\Gamma(1+2b^2-2ibP_1)\,\Gamma(\frac{1-b^2}{2}+ibP_1\pm ibP_2\pm ibP_3)}{\Gamma(1+2ibP_1)\,\Gamma(1-b^2+2ibP_1)\,\Gamma(\frac{1+b^2}{2}-ibP_1\pm ibP_2\pm ibP_3)},$$

together with the same equation for $b\to b^{-1}$. For $b^2\notin\mathbb{Q}$ these
determine $C_b$ up to a constant, which the two-point function then fixes. The
formula was found by Dorn and Otto [@liouville-cft/dornotto1994] and by Zamolodchikov and
Zamolodchikov [@liouville-cft/zz1996], derived from the bootstrap by Teschner [@liouville-cft/teschner1995], and
later proved from the path integral by Kupiainen, Rhodes and Vargas [@liouville-cft/krv2017].

### Correlation functions

Any correlator on a closed Riemann surface follows from a pair-of-pants
decomposition into $2g-2+n$ pairs of pants sewn along $3g-3+n$ cuffs. Each cuff
carries a factor of $\rho_0^{(b)}$ and each pair of pants a factor of $C_b$:

$$\langle V_{P_1}\cdots V_{P_n}\rangle_g=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}}\Big(\prod_a\mathrm{d}P_a\,\rho_0^{(b)}(P_a)\Big)\Big(\prod_{(j,k,l)}C_b(P_j,P_k,P_l)\Big)\big|\mathcal{F}^{(b)}_{g,n}(\mathbf{P}^{\rm ext};\mathbf{P}|\mathbf{m})\big|^2.$$

Here $\mathcal{F}^{(b)}_{g,n}$ are Virasoro conformal blocks, and the result does
not depend on the channel. The simplest cases are

$$\begin{aligned}\langle V_{P_1}(0)V_{P_2}(z,\bar z)V_{P_3}(1)V_{P_4}(\infty)\rangle={}&\int_0^\infty\mathrm{d}P\,\rho_0^{(b)}(P)\,C_b(P_1,P_2,P)\,C_b(P_3,P_4,P)\\&\times\mathcal{F}^{(b)}_{0,4}(P|z)\,\mathcal{F}^{(b)}_{0,4}(P|\bar z),\end{aligned}$$

$$\langle V_{P_1}(0)\rangle_{g=1}=\int_0^\infty\mathrm{d}P\,\rho_0^{(b)}(P)\,C_b(P_1,P,P)\,\mathcal{F}^{(b)}_{1,1}(P_1;P|q)\,\mathcal{F}^{(b)}_{1,1}(P_1;P|\bar q).$$

The torus partition function is the trace over the continuum, with characters
$\chi_P(\tau)=q^{P^2}/\eta(\tau)$. Up to a divergent factor from the volume of
the $\phi$ zero mode, it is the modular invariant

$$\int_0^\infty\mathrm{d}P\,|\chi_P(\tau)|^2=\frac{1}{4\sqrt{\tau_2}\,|\eta(\tau)|^2}.$$

### The double gamma function

**Definition.** $\Gamma_b(z)$ is the meromorphic function that depends
continuously on $b$ and satisfies the shift equations

$$\Gamma_b(z+b)=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}\,b^{bz-\frac{1}{2}}}{\Gamma(bz)}\,\Gamma_b(z),\qquad\Gamma_b(z+b^{-1})=\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}\,b^{-b^{-1}z+\frac{1}{2}}}{\Gamma(b^{-1}z)}\,\Gamma_b(z),$$

with the normalisation $\Gamma_b(\frac{Q}{2})=1$. Up to this normalisation it is
the double gamma function of Barnes [@liouville-cft/barnes1901] for periods $b$ and $b^{-1}$, and
$\Gamma_b=\Gamma_{b^{-1}}$.

**Integral representation.** For $\operatorname{Re}z>0$,

$$\log\Gamma_b(z)=\int_0^\infty\frac{\mathrm{d}t}{t}\left(\frac{e^{\frac{t}{2}(Q-2z)}-1}{4\sinh(\frac{bt}{2})\sinh(\frac{t}{2b})}-\frac{1}{8}(Q-2z)^2e^{-t}-\frac{Q-2z}{2t}\right).$$

The shift equations continue this to all of $\mathbb{C}$.

**Poles.** $\Gamma_b(z)$ has no zeros. Its poles are at
$z=-mb-nb^{-1}$ with $m,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$. They are simple for
$b^2\notin\mathbb{Q}$, and coincide to form higher-order poles for
$b^2\in\mathbb{Q}$. The residues are

$$\begin{aligned}\operatorname*{Res}_{z=-mb-nb^{-1}}\Gamma_b(z)={}&\frac{\Gamma_b(Q)}{(2\pi)^{\frac{m+n}{2}+1}}\,b^{\frac{1}{2}m(m+1)b^2-\frac{1}{2}n(n+1)b^{-2}-mn-\frac{1}{2}(n-m)}\\&\times\prod_{j=1}^{m}\Gamma(-jb^2)\prod_{k=1}^{n}\Gamma(-kb^{-2}-m).\end{aligned}$$

In particular $\operatorname{Res}_{z=0}\Gamma_b(z)=\Gamma_b(Q)/2\pi$.

**Double product.** With $\Omega_{m,n}=mb+nb^{-1}$, the Weierstrass form exhibits
the lattice of poles:

$$\Gamma_b(z)=\frac{\Gamma_b(Q)}{2\pi z}\,e^{a_bz+d_bz^2}\prod_{(m,n)\neq(0,0)}\frac{\exp\big(\frac{z}{\Omega_{m,n}}-\frac{z^2}{2\Omega_{m,n}^2}\big)}{1+z/\Omega_{m,n}},$$

$$a_b=\frac{b}{2}\log 2\pi+\frac{Q}{2}\log b-\gamma_{\rm E}\,b-\frac{A(b^2)}{b},\qquad d_b=\frac{\pi^2b^2}{12}-\frac{1}{2}\log b-\frac{B(b^2)}{2b^2}.$$

**Single product.** Resumming one direction of the lattice gives the form due to
Barnes [@liouville-cft/barnes1901] that is used for numerics at complex $z$ and $b$
[@liouville-cft/ak2023; @liouville-cft/cemr2025, App. B]:

$$\Gamma_b(z)=\frac{f_b(z)}{f_b(\frac{Q}{2})},$$

$$\begin{aligned}f_b(z)={}&(2\pi)^{\frac{bz}{2}}\,b^{\frac{z(Q-z)}{2}}\,\Gamma(bz)\,e^{-\frac{z}{b}A(b^2)-\frac{z^2}{2b^2}B(b^2)}\\&\times\prod_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{\Gamma(bz+mb^2)}{\Gamma(mb^2)}\,e^{-bz\,\psi(mb^2)-\frac{1}{2}(bz)^2\psi'(mb^2)}.\end{aligned}$$

The constants are built from the gamma modular forms $C(\tau)$ and $D(\tau)$ of
Barnes [@liouville-cft/barnes1901]:

$$A(\tau)=\frac{\tau}{2}\log(2\pi\tau)+\frac{1}{2}\log\tau-\tau\,C(\tau),\qquad B(\tau)=-\tau\log\tau-\tau^2D(\tau),$$

$$C(\tau)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\Big[\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\psi(k\tau)+\frac{\log 2\pi}{2\tau}-\frac{\log\Gamma(N\tau)}{\tau}+\frac{1}{2}\psi(N\tau)\Big],$$

$$D(\tau)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\Big[\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\psi'(k\tau)-\frac{\psi(N\tau)}{\tau}\Big].$$

**Related functions.** At $b=1$, $\Gamma_1(z)=(2\pi)^{\frac{z-1}{2}}/G(z)$ with
$G$ the Barnes $G$-function. The functions
$\Upsilon_b(z)=1/\big(\Gamma_b(z)\Gamma_b(Q-z)\big)$ and
$S_b(z)=\Gamma_b(z)/\Gamma_b(Q-z)$ are also common, and
$S_b(z+b)=2\sin(\pi bz)\,S_b(z)$.

### Analytic continuation in $b$

$\rho_0^{(b)}$ and $C_b$ are analytic in $b$ for $\operatorname{Re}b>0$. Since $c$
is invariant under $b\to b^{-1}$ and $b\to-b$, this half-plane covers every
$c\in\mathbb{C}\setminus(-\infty,1]$. The continuation preserves crossing
symmetry, and it defines the theory where the action is complex and the path
integral is unclear.

| $b$ | $c$ | Status |
|---|---|---|
| $b\in(0,1]$ | $c\geq 25$ | Unitary, real action |
| $b=e^{i\theta}$, $0<\lvert\theta\rvert<\frac{\pi}{2}$ | $c=1+24\cos^2\theta\in(1,25)$ | Unitary, $C_b>0$ for real momenta |
| $b\in e^{\frac{i\pi}{4}}\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ | $c\in 13+i\mathbb{R}$ | Used in the complex Liouville string |
| Generic $\operatorname{Re}b>0$ | $c\in\mathbb{C}\setminus(-\infty,1]$ | Crossing symmetric, no inner product |
| $b\in i\mathbb{R}$ | $c\leq 1$ | Continuation fails |

For complex $c$ there is no inner product, since $L_n^\dagger=L_{-n}$ is
incompatible with a complex central charge. The real $P$ contour remains valid:
for real external momenta, the poles of the integrand stay a distance
$\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Re}Q>0$ from the real axis.

The continuation does not reach $c\leq 1$. For $b\in i\mathbb{R}$ with irrational
$b^2$, the pole lattice $-mb-nb^{-1}$ would be dense on the imaginary axis, so
$\Gamma_b$ does not exist, and Liouville correlators have no well-defined limit.

### Analytic continuation in $P$

$\rho_0^{(b)}$ is entire in $P$ and $C_b$ is meromorphic in each momentum. For
generic momenta and $b^2\notin\mathbb{Q}$, $C_b$ has

- zeros at $P_k=\pm\frac{i}{2}(rb+sb^{-1})$ with $r,s\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$, where
  $V_{P_k}$ is degenerate;
- simple poles at $\pm P_1\pm P_2\pm P_3=i(r+\frac{1}{2})b+i(s+\frac{1}{2})b^{-1}$
  with $r,s\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$, which are associated with multi-twist operators.

Correlators are first defined at real external momenta and then continued. The
block decomposition has poles in each internal momentum at

$$P=\pm P_j\pm P_k\pm i\big((r+\tfrac{1}{2})b+(s+\tfrac{1}{2})b^{-1}\big),\qquad r,s\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},$$

for the external legs $j,k$ on the same pair of pants. These stay off the real
axis while $\lvert\operatorname{Im}(P_j\pm P_k)\rvert<\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Re}Q$,
which is $\frac{Q}{2}$ for real $b$. Beyond that, poles cross the contour, and
analyticity requires discrete contributions. On the sphere,

$$\begin{aligned}\langle V_{P_1}(0)V_{P_2}(z,\bar z)V_{P_3}(1)V_{P_4}(\infty)\rangle&=\int_0^\infty\mathrm{d}P\,I(P)+2\pi i\sum_{P_*}\operatorname*{Res}_{P=P_*}I(P),\\ I(P)&=\rho_0^{(b)}(P)\,C_b(P_1,P_2,P)\,C_b(P_3,P_4,P)\,\mathcal{F}^{(b)}_{0,4}(P|z)\,\mathcal{F}^{(b)}_{0,4}(P|\bar z),\end{aligned}$$

where the sum runs over the poles that started above the real axis and have moved
below it. $I$ is even in $P$, so this already accounts for the mirror poles at
$-P_*$. For example, take $P_1=i\eta_1$ and $P_2=i\eta_2$ with
$\eta_1+\eta_2>\frac{Q}{2}$. The first pole to cross is at
$P_*=i(\frac{Q}{2}-\eta_1-\eta_2)$. This is the familiar condition
$\alpha_1+\alpha_2<\frac{Q}{2}$, with exchanged operator
$\alpha=\alpha_1+\alpha_2$.

Operators with $P\notin\mathbb{R}$ are not in the spectrum: for example, those
with real weights below $\frac{c-1}{24}$ are not normalisable. They do not appear
as internal states of generic correlators, but their own correlators are well
defined by this continuation.

### Coulomb gas poles on $\Sigma_{g,n}$

On a closed oriented Riemann surface of genus $g$ with $n$ punctures, correlators
have poles where the background charge is saturated:

$$\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_j=Q(1-g)-rb-sb^{-1},\qquad\alpha_j=\frac{Q}{2}+iP_j,\qquad r,s\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.$$

Since $V_{-P}=V_P$, this holds for every choice of signs of the momenta. With
$2g-2+n=-\chi(\Sigma_{g,n})$, the condition is

$$\pm P_1\pm P_2\pm\cdots\pm P_n=i\Big(\frac{Q}{2}(2g-2+n)+rb+sb^{-1}\Big).$$

| $(g,n)$ | Poles | Origin |
|---|---|---|
| $(0,3)$ | $\pm P_1\pm P_2\pm P_3=i(r+\frac{1}{2})b+i(s+\frac{1}{2})b^{-1}$ | Poles of $C_b$ |
| $(0,4)$ | $\pm P_1\pm P_2\pm P_3\pm P_4=i(r+1)b+i(s+1)b^{-1}$ | Pinching of the $P$ contour |
| $(1,1)$ | $\pm P_1=i(r+\frac{1}{2})b+i(s+\frac{1}{2})b^{-1}$ | Factors $\Gamma_b(\frac{Q}{2}\pm iP_1)$ in $C_b(P_1,P,P)$ |

**Path integral.** Shift the zero mode, $\phi\to\phi+\phi_0$. With
$\int\sqrt{g}\,R=8\pi(1-g)$ and $\mathcal{A}=\int\mathrm{d}^2x\sqrt{g}\,e^{2b\phi}$, the
integral over $\phi_0$ is

$$\int\mathrm{d}\phi_0\;e^{2(\sum_j\alpha_j-Q(1-g))\phi_0-\mu\mathcal{A}e^{2b\phi_0}}=\frac{1}{2b}\,\Gamma(-N)\,(\mu\mathcal{A})^{N},\qquad N=\frac{Q(1-g)-\sum_j\alpha_j}{b}.$$

The poles at $N=r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ come from the region $\phi_0\to-\infty$,
where the potential switches off. The residue is a free-field correlator with $r$
insertions of the screening operator $e^{2b\phi}$. Duality $b\to b^{-1}$ adds the
dual screening operator $e^{2b^{-1}\phi}$, which accounts for $s$. At $r=s=0$ the
residue is the free boson correlator with background charge $Q$.

**Bootstrap.** In the block decomposition, these poles come from the singularities
of $C_b$. On a general surface, poles of $C_b$ on opposite sides of an internal
$P$ contour pinch it. For $(0,4)$, a pole of $C_b(P_1,P_2,P)$ meets a pole of
$C_b(P_3,P_4,P)$. For $(1,1)$ the poles are already in the integrand, and at
$r=s=0$ the operator becomes the identity, so the residue is the torus partition
function:

$$\langle V_{\frac{iQ}{2}-i\varepsilon}\rangle_{g=1}\approx\frac{1}{\pi\varepsilon}\int_0^\infty\mathrm{d}P\,|\chi_P(\tau)|^2.$$

### Relation to the standard normalisation

The operators $e^{2\alpha\phi}$ have the Zamolodchikov–Zamolodchikov form of the
DOZZ formula [@liouville-cft/zz1996]. With $\lambda=\pi\mu\,\gamma(b^2)\,b^{2-2b^2}$ and
$\gamma(x)=\Gamma(x)/\Gamma(1-x)$,

$$C^{\rm ZZ}(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)=\lambda^{\frac{Q-\sigma}{b}}\,\frac{\Upsilon_b'(0)\prod_{j=1}^{3}\Upsilon_b(2\alpha_j)}{\Upsilon_b(\sigma-Q)\prod_{j=1}^{3}\Upsilon_b(\sigma-2\alpha_j)},\qquad\sigma=\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3.$$

It has unit residue at $\sigma=Q$, in agreement with the free-field
normalisation. The two normalisations are related by

$$C^{\rm ZZ}(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)=\kappa_b\,N(P_1)N(P_2)N(P_3)\,C_b(P_1,P_2,P_3),$$

$$N(P)=\lambda^{-\frac{iP}{b}}\,\frac{\Gamma_b(Q-2iP)}{\Gamma_b(-2iP)},\qquad\kappa_b=\lambda^{-\frac{Q}{2b}}\,\frac{2\sqrt{2}\,\pi\,\Gamma_b(Q)}{\Gamma_b(2Q)}.$$

So $e^{2\alpha\phi}=\kappa_b^{1/3}N(P)\,V_P$, and the reflection relation is
$e^{2\alpha\phi}=\frac{N(P)}{N(-P)}\,e^{2(Q-\alpha)\phi}$.

theories.name: Monster CFT
theories.summary: The holomorphic CFT with $c = 24$, partition function $J(\tau) = j(\tau) - 744$ and no weight-1 states, built by Frenkel, Lepowsky and Meurman [@monster-cft/flm1984; @monster-cft/flm1988] as a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ orbifold of the Leech lattice theory. Its automorphism group is the Monster.
theories.description:
A holomorphic (chiral, self-dual) CFT has a single irreducible module, so its character is
modular invariant by itself when $c$ is a multiple of 24. At $c = 24$ modular invariance fixes it to
$J(\tau) + N$, where $N$ is the number of weight-1 states [@monster-cft/witten2007, Sec. 3.1]; the Monster CFT is
the case $N = 0$:
$$Z(\tau) = J(\tau) = j(\tau) - 744 = q^{-1} + 196884\,q + 21493760\,q^2 + 864299970\,q^3 + \dots$$
It has $c_L = 24$ and $c_R = 0$. With no currents, its Virasoro primaries start at weight 2: of the
196884 weight-2 states one is the stress tensor and $196883$ are primaries in the smallest
non-trivial irreducible representation of the Monster group $\mathbb{M}$. This realizes McKay's
observation $196884 = 1 + 196883$. The weight-2 space carries a commutative non-associative algebra,
a slight modification of the 196884-dimensional algebra Griess used to construct $\mathbb{M}$.

**Construction.** Take the 24 chiral bosons on the Leech lattice $\Lambda$ (the
Leech lattice CFT, $Z = J + 24$) and orbifold by a lift of $X \to -X$. In Schellekens' description [@monster-cft/schellekens1993]
the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ orbifold has four primaries of spins $0, 1, \tfrac32, 2$ (the even and odd
untwisted states and the odd and even twisted states). Adding the spin-2 simple current to the chiral
algebra gives a new holomorphic theory with $N_{\rm twisted} = \tfrac12 N_{\rm lattice} - 12$
weight-1 states, which vanishes for the Leech lattice. Frenkel, Lepowsky and Meurman (FLM) [@monster-cft/flm1984; @monster-cft/flm1988] built
$V^\natural$ this way, and showed that $\mathbb{M}$ is exactly the group of automorphisms of the
vertex algebra commuting with the Virasoro action. Dixon, Ginsparg and Harvey [@monster-cft/dgh1988] described the
construction as a CFT orbifold (Schellekens [@monster-cft/schellekens1993] attributes the formula for $N_{\rm twisted}$ to them),
and argued that a fermionic (spin) lift of $V^\natural$ has $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal
symmetry; a supercurrent was constructed explicitly by Moore and Singh [@monster-cft/ms2025].

**Monstrous moonshine.** Conway and Norton [@monster-cft/conwaynorton1979] conjectured that for each $m \in \mathbb{M}$ the
McKay–Thompson series $T_m(\tau) = q^{-1}\sum_n \mathrm{tr}_{V^\natural_n}(m)\, q^n$ is the normalized
principal modulus (Hauptmodul) of a genus-zero group $\Gamma_m$; for the identity, $T_e = J$.
Borcherds [@monster-cft/borcherds1992] proved this for the FLM module. For example $T_{2B} = q^{-1}\prod_{n>0}(1-q^{2n-1})^{24} + 24 = q^{-1} + 276q - 2048q^2 + \dots$, with $\Gamma_{2B} = \Gamma_0(2)$.

**Uniqueness.** FLM [@monster-cft/flm1988] conjectured that $V^\natural$ is the unique vertex operator algebra with
central charge 24 that is self-dual and has no non-zero states of weight 1. This is the only open
case of the classification of holomorphic $c = 24$ theories. Dong, Griess and Lam [@monster-cft/dgl2007]
proved uniqueness under additional assumptions.

**Three-dimensional gravity.** Witten [@monster-cft/witten2007] proposed that pure three-dimensional gravity with negative
cosmological constant is dual to holomorphically factorized CFTs with $c_L$, $c_R$ multiples of 24
whose partition functions are "extremal". At $c = 24$ (the most negative cosmological constant) the
holomorphic factor has partition function $J$ and, if the FLM conjecture holds, is $V^\natural$. In
this proposal the 196883 weight-2 primaries, combined with antiholomorphic factors, create black holes, and $\ln 196883 \approx 12.19$ is close to the Bekenstein–Hawking
value $4\pi \approx 12.57$. This is a proposal, not an established duality.

theories.name: $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ WZW model
aliases: Worldsheet theory of strings on $AdS_3$ with NS–NS flux
WZW model on the universal cover of $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$
theories.summary: The WZW model on the universal cover of $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$, Lorentzian $AdS_3$, at real level $k>2$: $c=\frac{3k}{k-2}$. Its spectrum [@sl2r-wzw/mo2001a] has continuous and discrete representations and all their spectral flows. The worldsheet theory of strings on $AdS_3$ with NS–NS flux.
theories.description:
The target of this WZW model is the group manifold $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$, the hyperboloid that is Lorentzian $AdS_3$,
with metric $-\cosh^2\rho\,dt^2+d\rho^2+\sinh^2\rho\,d\phi^2$ in global coordinates. Maldacena and Ooguri [@sl2r-wzw/mo2001a] take its
universal cover, so that global time $t$ is not compact. The level $k$ is real, since $H^3$ of $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$
vanishes; large $k$ is the semiclassical limit, and $k>2$ is assumed. The currents generate two copies of
$\widehat{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})_k$,
$$[J^3_n,J^3_m]=-\tfrac{k}{2}n\,\delta_{n+m,0},\qquad[J^3_n,J^\pm_m]=\pm J^\pm_{n+m},\qquad[J^+_n,J^-_m]=-2J^3_{n+m}+kn\,\delta_{n+m,0},$$
and the Sugawara stress tensor has $c=\frac{3k}{k-2}$. In global $AdS_3$ the spacetime energy is $E=J^3_0+\bar
J^3_0$ and the angular momentum is $\ell=J^3_0-\bar J^3_0$.

The kinetic term has indefinite signature, because of the timelike direction, so the space of states contains states
with negative $L_0$ and states with negative norm. Representations of $\widehat{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})_k$ are not unitary
except for the trivial one, and the model cannot be continued to a Euclidean worldsheet because its Hamiltonian is
not positive definite [@sl2r-wzw/mo2001a]. In string theory this is acceptable: the requirement is that physical
states have non-negative norm after the Virasoro constraints are imposed. For bosonic strings on $AdS_3\times M$
with NS–NS flux, with a **unitary** CFT for $M$ of central charge $26-\frac{3k}{k-2}$ (which requires $c_M \geq 0$, i.e. $k \geq \frac{52}{23}$, a stronger condition than $k > 2$; derived), the no-ghost theorem states that the
constraints $(L_n+L^M_n-\delta_{n,0})|\text{phys}\rangle=0$, $n\geq0$, remove all negative-norm states from the
continuous representations and from the discrete ones with $0<j<\frac{k}{2}$, including all their spectral flows.

### Spectrum
The unitary representations of the zero modes that appear have Casimir $-j(j-1)$: the discrete series
$\mathcal{D}^\pm_j$, with $J^3_0=\pm j,\pm(j+1),\dots$, and the continuous series $\mathcal{C}^\alpha_j$ with
$j=\frac12+is$ and $J^3_0\in\alpha+\mathbb{Z}$, $0\leq\alpha<1$. As $k\to\infty$ the model becomes quantum mechanics
on $AdS_3$, and $L^2(AdS_3)$ is spanned by $\mathcal{C}\otimes\mathcal{C}$ and by
$\mathcal{D}^\pm_j\otimes\mathcal{D}^\pm_j$ with $j>\frac12$. The current-algebra modules $\hat{\mathcal{D}}^\pm_j$,
$\hat{\mathcal{C}}^\alpha_j$ built on them have primaries with $L_0=-\frac{j(j-1)}{k-2}$. Spectral flow by
$w\in\mathbb{Z}$,
$$\tilde J^3_n=J^3_n-\tfrac{k}{2}w\,\delta_{n,0},\qquad\tilde J^\pm_n=J^\pm_{n\pm w},\qquad\tilde L_n=L_n+wJ^3_n-\tfrac{k}{4}w^2\delta_{n,0},$$
maps these to inequivalent modules whose $L_0$ is not bounded below, unlike for $SU(2)$. The proposal of Maldacena
and Ooguri [@sl2r-wzw/mo2001a] is
$$\mathcal{H}=\bigoplus_{w\in\mathbb{Z}}\Big[\int_{1/2}^{(k-1)/2}dj\,\hat{\mathcal{D}}^w_j\otimes\hat{\mathcal{D}}^w_j\;\oplus\;\int_{\frac12+i\mathbb{R}}dj\int_0^1d\alpha\,\hat{\mathcal{C}}^w_{j,\alpha}\otimes\hat{\mathcal{C}}^w_{j,\alpha}\Big],$$
with equal flow on the left and right, as required on the universal cover. Flow by one unit maps
$\hat{\mathcal{D}}^+_{\tilde j}$ to $\hat{\mathcal{D}}^-_{k/2-\tilde j}$, so $j>\frac12$ from harmonic analysis
forces $j<\frac{k-1}{2}$, stricter than the no-ghost bound $j<\frac{k}{2}$. On the universal cover the discrete $j$
takes continuous values; on the single cover it would be discrete.

In string theory the discrete modules and their flows give short strings with discrete energies. The flowed
continuous modules give long strings, of winding $w$ near the boundary, with energy $J^3_0$ given below; the
unflowed continuous modules give only the tachyon. With spectral flow, the masses of short strings are no longer
bounded above. Three checks support the proposal. Summing the discrete characters over $\frac12<j<\frac{k-1}{2}$ and
over $w$ reproduces, after continuation and up to contact terms, the partition function of the $H_3^+$ model
computed by Gawedzki [@sl2r-wzw/gawedzki1991]. The one-loop partition function on thermal $AdS_3$ reproduces the spectrum
[@sl2r-wzw/mos2001]. Four-point functions, obtained from the $H_3^+$ model by analytic continuation, factorize on these states
exactly when the dual boundary CFT says they should, and in an $N$-point function of $x$-basis operators with
$w_i\geq0$ the windings obey $w_i-\sum_{j\neq i}w_j\leq N-2$ [@sl2r-wzw/mo2002].

### Superstrings and the $k=1$ point
For superstrings on $AdS_3\times S^3\times T^4$ with pure NS–NS flux, the RNS worldsheet contains the supersymmetric
$\widehat{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})^{(1)}_k$, a bosonic $\widehat{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})_{k+2}$ plus three free fermions, where
$k$ is the NS–NS flux; this description needs $k\geq2$. For one unit of flux, $k=1$, Eberhardt, Gaberdiel and
Gopakumar [@sl2r-wzw/egg2019] use instead the hybrid formalism with a $\mathfrak{psu}(1,1|2)_1$ WZW model. Its string spectrum has no
long-string continuum except the bottom of it and no discrete representations, and it matches the large-$N$ limit of
the symmetric orbifold $\mathrm{Sym}^N(T^4)$; they interpret this point as the tensionless limit. The $k=1$ point is
therefore not an instance of the bosonic model on this page.

### Status
The space of states above is a proposal, supported by the no-ghost theorem, the partition functions and the
factorization of four-point functions. In 2005 Ribault and Teschner [@sl2r-wzw/rt2005] described the definition and analytic properties
of correlators with more than three insertions as not yet under control.

theories.name: $\mathcal{N}=1$ super-Liouville theory
theories.summary: The $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric extension of Liouville CFT, with $c=\frac32+3Q^2$. A fermionic theory of a boson and its superpartner fermion, with NS and R sectors, continuous spectra and exactly known three-point functions.
theories.description:
$\mathcal{N}=1$ super-Liouville theory is the supersymmetric extension of Liouville CFT, first considered by Polyakov [@super-liouville/polyakov1981]. Its superfield $\Phi=\phi+i\theta\psi+i\bar\theta\bar\psi+i\theta\bar\theta F$ contains a real boson $\phi$ with a linear dilaton and its fermionic superpartner $(\psi,\bar\psi)$. It arises from the quantisation of two-dimensional supergravity, and describes 2d supergravity induced by supersymmetric matter, as Liouville CFT does for gravity. Like Liouville it is non-compact, with continuous spectra. This page follows Fukuda and Hosomichi [@super-liouville/fh2002].

$$c=\tfrac32\hat c=\tfrac32+3Q^2,\qquad\hat c=1+2Q^2,\qquad Q=b+b^{-1}.$$

The interaction is normalised as $e^{b\phi}$, not $e^{2b\phi}$ as in Liouville CFT, and at the same $b$ the central charge is not the bosonic $1+6Q^2$.

It is a fermionic theory. The fermion $\psi$ and the supercurrent $T_F=i(\psi\partial\phi-Q\partial\psi)$, of weight $\frac32$, are local fields, and the primaries fall into a Neveu–Schwarz (NS) sector, local with respect to $T_F$, and a Ramond (R) sector, around which $T_F$ is double-valued. The NS primaries are $V_\alpha=e^{\alpha\phi}$, with superpartners at weight $h_\alpha+\frac12$, where

$$h_\alpha=\bar h_\alpha=\frac{\alpha(Q-\alpha)}{2}=\frac{Q^2}{8}+\frac{p^2}{2},\qquad\alpha=\frac{Q}{2}+ip,\quad p\in\mathbb{R}.$$

The R primaries are $\Theta^{\epsilon\bar\epsilon}_\alpha=\sigma^\epsilon\bar\sigma^{\bar\epsilon}e^{\alpha\phi}$ ($\epsilon,\bar\epsilon=\pm$), with spin fields $\sigma^\pm$ of weight $\frac{1}{16}$, so $h=h_\alpha+\frac{1}{16}=\frac{c}{24}+\frac{p^2}{2}$. In the fermionic theory the R-sector superprimaries come in a pair, $R^{(+)}_P \sim \mu\,e^{\alpha\phi}$ and $R^{(-)}_P \sim \sigma\,e^{\alpha\phi}$ with $\mu$, $\sigma$ the disorder and spin fields, of equal weights [@super-liouville/dly2025, Eqs. (2.15)–(2.16)]; for $p \neq 0$, $G_0^2 = L_0 - \frac{c}{24} = \frac{p^2}{2}$ is invertible and $G_0$ reverses fermion parity, so the Ramond ground states form a doublet of opposite parity (derived). Keeping a single combination of the four fields $\Theta^{\epsilon\bar\epsilon}_\alpha$ at each $\alpha$, as Fredenhagen and Wellig [@super-liouville/fw2007] do by analogy with the free fermion, describes a projected (bosonized) theory rather than the fermionic one. The continua start at $p=0$, with $h=\frac{Q^2}{8}=\frac{2c-3}{48}$ in the NS sector and $h=\frac{c}{24}$ in the R sector.

Degenerate representations sit at $\alpha_{r,s}=\frac12(Q-rb-sb^{-1})$, $r,s\geq1$, with a null vector at level $\frac{rs}{2}$; they are NS for $r+s$ even and R for $r+s$ odd. The simplest non-trivial one is the R field $\Theta_{-b/2}$.

Reflection $\alpha\to Q-\alpha$ identifies $V_\alpha=D(\alpha)V_{Q-\alpha}$ (likewise for the superpartners) and $\epsilon\bar\epsilon\,\Theta^{\epsilon\bar\epsilon}_\alpha=\tilde D(\alpha)\,\Theta^{-\epsilon,-\bar\epsilon}_{Q-\alpha}$, so the reflection of an R field also flips $\epsilon,\bar\epsilon$. With $\lambda=\mu\pi\gamma(\frac{bQ}{2})\,b^{1-b^2}$ and $\gamma(x)=\Gamma(x)/\Gamma(1-x)$,

$$D(\alpha)=\lambda^{\frac{Q-2\alpha}{b}}\frac{\Upsilon_{\rm NS}(2\alpha)}{\Upsilon_{\rm NS}(2Q-2\alpha)},\qquad\tilde D(\alpha)=\lambda^{\frac{Q-2\alpha}{b}}\frac{\Upsilon_{\rm R}(2\alpha)}{\Upsilon_{\rm R}(2Q-2\alpha)},$$

$$\Upsilon_{\rm NS}(x)=\Upsilon\big(\tfrac{x}{2}\big)\Upsilon\big(\tfrac{x+Q}{2}\big),\qquad\Upsilon_{\rm R}(x)=\Upsilon\big(\tfrac{x+b}{2}\big)\Upsilon\big(\tfrac{x+b^{-1}}{2}\big),$$

where $\Upsilon$ is the function of the DOZZ formula. They satisfy $D(\alpha)D(Q-\alpha)=\tilde D(\alpha)\tilde D(Q-\alpha)=1$. In terms of gamma functions, $D(\alpha)=-\big(\mu\pi\gamma(\frac{bQ}{2})\big)^{\frac{Q-2\alpha}{b}}\frac{\Gamma(bx)\Gamma(b^{-1}x)}{\Gamma(-bx)\Gamma(-b^{-1}x)}$ with $x=\alpha-\frac{Q}{2}$.

### Three-point functions

The three-point function of NS primaries is, up to the standard coordinate dependence,

$$\langle V_{\alpha_1}V_{\alpha_2}V_{\alpha_3}\rangle=\lambda^{\frac{Q-\sum_i\alpha_i}{b}}\,\frac{\Upsilon_{\rm NS}'(0)\,\Upsilon_{\rm NS}(2\alpha_1)\Upsilon_{\rm NS}(2\alpha_2)\Upsilon_{\rm NS}(2\alpha_3)}{\Upsilon_{\rm NS}(\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3-Q)\,\Upsilon_{\rm NS}(\alpha_1+\alpha_2-\alpha_3)\,\Upsilon_{\rm NS}(\alpha_2+\alpha_3-\alpha_1)\,\Upsilon_{\rm NS}(\alpha_3+\alpha_1-\alpha_2)}.$$

Superconformal symmetry gives all other NS three-point functions from this one and from $\langle\psi\bar\psi V_{\alpha_1}V_{\alpha_2}V_{\alpha_3}\rangle$, whose denominator is built from $\Upsilon_{\rm R}$ [@super-liouville/fh2002, Eq. (2.58)]. Three-point functions with two R fields are given in [@super-liouville/fh2002, Eq. (2.64)]. The NS function has poles where $\sum_i(\alpha_i\ \text{or}\ Q-\alpha_i)=Q-mb-nb^{-1}$ with $m,n\geq0$ and $m+n$ even, reflecting the fermionic screening operator $\psi\bar\psi e^{b\phi}$.

The structure constants were proposed by Rashkov and Stanishkov [@super-liouville/rs1996] from their pole structure, and derived by Poghossian [@super-liouville/poghossian1997], in both sectors, from four-point functions with the degenerate R field $\Theta_{-b/2}$ (the method Teschner [@super-liouville/teschner1995] used for Liouville). Fukuda and Hosomichi [@super-liouville/fh2002] rederived them in the form above.

### Related theories

At $b=1$ ($\hat c=9$, $c=\frac{27}{2}$), super-Liouville theory together with a free $\hat c=1$ superfield $(X,\chi)$ is the worldsheet theory of the two-dimensional type 0A and 0B strings [@super-liouville/nakayama2004, Sec. 7.3]. As $c\to\frac32$ ($b\to i$) its NS three-point functions have a limit, which coincides with the limit of the $\mathcal{N}=1$ superconformal minimal models [@super-liouville/fw2007]: a non-rational theory at $c=\frac32$, the supersymmetric analogue of the Runkel–Watts theory.

theories.name: Toda CFT
theories.summary: The $\mathfrak{sl}(N)$ generalisation of Liouville CFT ($N=2$): $N-1$ scalars with exponential interactions, $\mathcal{W}_N$ symmetry and a continuous spectrum. Three-point functions are known in closed form only when one field is semi-degenerate.
theories.description:
Toda CFT is the theory of an $(N-1)$-component scalar $\varphi$ valued in the Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak{sl}(N)$, with one exponential interaction for each simple root $e_k$. Liouville CFT is the case $N=2$. Like Liouville it is non-compact and non-rational, with a continuum of scalar primaries. This page is a single entry with parameters $N$ and $b$, in the conventions of Fateev and Litvinov [@toda-cft/fl2007]: $(\cdot,\cdot)$ is the inner product on the root space and $\rho$ is the Weyl vector, with $(\rho,\rho)=\frac{N(N^2-1)}{12}$.

$$Q=\big(b+b^{-1}\big)\rho,\qquad c=N-1+12(Q,Q)=(N-1)\big(1+N(N+1)(b+b^{-1})^2\big).$$

The Miura transformation builds from $\varphi$ holomorphic currents $W_k$ of spin $k=2,\dots,N$, with $W_2=T$. They form the $\mathcal{W}_N$ algebra, so the symmetry is $\mathcal{W}_N\otimes\overline{\mathcal{W}}_N$. The central charge is invariant under $b\to b^{-1}$, and the theory has dual screening charges $e^{b^{-1}(e_k,\varphi)}$ with a dual cosmological constant $\tilde\mu$.

The primaries are $V_\alpha=e^{(\alpha,\varphi)}$, labelled by a vector momentum $\alpha$, with $h=\bar h=\frac12(\alpha,2Q-\alpha)$. The physical spectrum is $\alpha=Q+ip$ with $p$ a real vector, for which the weights are real and non-negative. It is diagonal: one $\mathcal{W}_N\otimes\overline{\mathcal{W}}_N$ representation for each Weyl orbit of $p$, integrated over $p$ [@toda-cft/cgt2015, Eq. (6.2)]. The character of a continuous representation is $q^{(p,p)/2}/\eta(\tau)^{N-1}$ ([@toda-cft/fr2010, Eq. (2.22)], at $\alpha=Q+ip$). The continuum starts at $p=0$, with $h=\frac12(Q,Q)=\frac{c-N+1}{24}$; at $N=2$ this is Liouville's $\frac{c-1}{24}$.

Momenta related by the Weyl group acting on $\alpha-Q$ have the same $\mathcal{W}_N$ charges, and the fields agree up to a reflection amplitude ($\gamma(x)=\Gamma(x)/\Gamma(1-x)$, product over positive roots):

$$V_{Q+w(\alpha-Q)}=\frac{A(Q+w(\alpha-Q))}{A(\alpha)}\,V_\alpha,\qquad A(\alpha)=\big(\pi\mu\gamma(b^2)\big)^{\frac{(\alpha-Q,\rho)}{b}}\prod_{e>0}\Gamma\big(1-b(\alpha-Q,e)\big)\,\Gamma\big(-b^{-1}(\alpha-Q,e)\big).$$

Completely degenerate fields have $\alpha=-b\Omega_1-b^{-1}\Omega_2$, with $\Omega_{1,2}$ dominant integral weights; their OPE with any primary contains finitely many primaries. The semi-degenerate fields $\alpha=\kappa\omega_{N-1}$ and $\alpha=\kappa\omega_1$ ($\omega_k$ the fundamental weights) are degenerate at level one.

### Three-point functions

For $N\geq3$ the general three-point function is not known. Unlike in Liouville CFT, the four-point function of a completely degenerate field with three generic fields does not obey an ordinary Fuchsian differential equation of order $N$, and $\mathcal{W}_N$ symmetry does not reduce higher-point functions of $\mathcal{W}_N$ primaries to their three-point functions, because the descendants $(W_{-1})^nV_\alpha$ enter independently. When one field is semi-degenerate, Fateev and Litvinov [@toda-cft/fl2007, Eq. (1.39)] derived

$$C(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\kappa\omega_{N-1})=\big[\pi\mu\gamma(b^2)b^{2-2b^2}\big]^{\frac{(2Q-\sum_i\alpha_i,\rho)}{b}}\,\frac{\Upsilon(b)^{N-1}\,\Upsilon(\kappa)\prod_{e>0}\Upsilon\big((Q-\alpha_1,e)\big)\Upsilon\big((Q-\alpha_2,e)\big)}{\prod_{i,j=1}^{N}\Upsilon\big(\frac{\kappa}{N}+(\alpha_1-Q,h_i)+(\alpha_2-Q,h_j)\big)}.$$

Here $h_k=\omega_1-e_1-\dots-e_{k-1}$ are the weights of the fundamental representation, $\Upsilon$ is the function of the DOZZ formula, normalised by $\Upsilon(\frac{b+b^{-1}}{2})=1$, and $\sum_i\alpha_i=\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\kappa\omega_{N-1}$. The case $\alpha_3=\kappa\omega_1$ follows from $h_k\to-h_{N+1-k}$. With a semi-degenerate field, the four-point function with the completely degenerate field $V_{-b\omega_1}$ obeys a Fuchsian equation of order $N$, solved by hypergeometric functions of type $(N,N-1)$. For $N=3$, Fateev and Litvinov [@toda-cft/fl2009, Sec. 3] also give fields degenerate at higher level as Coulomb-type integrals.

For imaginary $b$ ($c\leq N-1$) Dupic, Estienne and Ikhlef [@toda-cft/dei2019] computed the semi-degenerate structure constants by the conformal bootstrap; they are not the analytic continuation of the formula above.

### AGT relation

Alday, Gaiotto and Tachikawa [@toda-cft/agt2010] conjectured that Liouville correlators on a punctured Riemann surface equal integrals of $|Z|^2$, with $Z$ the full Nekrasov partition function of a four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ $SU(2)$ superconformal theory of the corresponding class, at $\epsilon_1=b$, $\epsilon_2=b^{-1}$. The sphere with four punctures gives $SU(2)$ with four flavours, and $b=1$ gives Pestun's $S^4$ partition function [@toda-cft/pestun2007]. Wyllard [@toda-cft/wyllard2009] extended the conjecture to $A_{N-1}$ Toda CFT and conformal $\mathcal{N}=2$ $SU(N)$ quiver gauge theories. A puncture with $U(1)$ flavour symmetry corresponds to a semi-degenerate field and a full puncture to a generic $\alpha$; the one-loop factors match the semi-degenerate structure constants up to normalisation, and the one-instanton term of $SU(3)$ with six fundamentals matches the $\mathcal{W}_3$ conformal block.

### $\mathcal{W}_N$ minimal models

At imaginary $b$ with $b^2=-p'/p$, the central charge becomes $(N-1)\big(1-N(N+1)\frac{(p-p')^2}{pp'}\big)$, that of the $\mathcal{W}_N$ minimal models. Bouwknegt and Schoutens [@toda-cft/bs1993, Sec. 6.2] review the argument that Toda theory at these couplings nevertheless cannot be identified directly with the minimal model: projections are needed, and the Toda spectrum gives only a subset of the minimal-model primaries. The minimal models have $c<N-1$, with supremum $N-1$, reached by Toda at $b=i$. Fredenhagen [@toda-cft/fredenhagen2011] showed that the disc one-point functions of Toda CFT have a limit at $c=N-1$ that agrees, up to normalisation of the fields, with the limit of the $\mathcal{W}_N$ minimal models.

theories.name: 3d ABJM theory, $U(N)_k \times U(N)_{-k}$
theories.summary: The $\mathcal{N}=6$ Chern–Simons-matter SCFT $U(N)_k\times U(N)_{-k}$ on $N$ M2-branes probing $\mathbb{C}^4/\mathbb{Z}_k$, dual to M-theory on $AdS_4\times S^7/\mathbb{Z}_k$. Supersymmetry is enhanced to $\mathcal{N}=8$ at $k = 1, 2$.
theories.description:
Two $U(N)$ Chern–Simons gauge fields at levels $k$ and $-k$ are coupled to two
bifundamental hypermultiplets. In $\mathcal{N}=2$ language the matter is the chiral
superfields $\mathcal{A}_{1,2}$ in $(\mathbf{N},\bar{\mathbf{N}})$ and $\mathcal{B}_{1,2}$ in
$(\bar{\mathbf{N}},\mathbf{N})$, with the quartic superpotential below. The theory has
$\mathcal{N}=6$ superconformal symmetry (12 real Poincaré supercharges) and a parity
symmetry that also exchanges the two gauge groups. The coupling is $1/k$: at large $N$
with $\lambda = N/k$ fixed there is a 't Hooft expansion, weakly coupled for
$k \gg N$ and strongly coupled for $k \ll N$. For $N = k = 1$ the theory is free.

Aharony, Bergman, Jafferis and Maldacena [@abjm-3d/abjm2008] argued that the theory describes $N$ M2-branes
probing $\mathbb{C}^4/\mathbb{Z}_k$. At large $N$ it is dual to M-theory on
$AdS_4\times S^7/\mathbb{Z}_k$, which is weakly curved for $N \gg k^5$. For larger $k$
the M-theory circle is small and type IIA string theory on $AdS_4\times\mathbb{CP}^3$ is
the better description; it is weakly curved for $k \ll N$ and also describes the 't Hooft
limit.

At $k = 1$ and $k = 2$ the theory has $\mathcal{N}=8$ superconformal symmetry
($\mathfrak{osp}(8|4)$, 16 supercharges, $SO(8)_R$), which is not visible in the
Lagrangian. ABJM [@abjm-3d/abjm2008] conjectured it, noting that at $k = 1, 2$ monopole ('t Hooft) operators
give extra conserved currents, and Bashkirov and Kapustin [@abjm-3d/bashkirov2011] showed, using monopole
operators, that the hidden supersymmetry is present. At $k = 1$ the theory describes $N$
M2-branes in flat space. For $N > 1$ it flows to a free sector (eight real scalars and
eight Majorana fermions, the centre-of-mass motion) times a strongly coupled interacting
SCFT. At $k = 2$ it describes M2-branes probing $\mathbb{R}^8/\mathbb{Z}_2$.

Aharony, Bergman and Jafferis [@abjm-3d/abj2008] generalized the construction to the $\mathcal{N}=6$ ABJ
theories $U(N+l)_k\times U(N)_{-k}$. They describe $N$ M2-branes on
$\mathbb{C}^4/\mathbb{Z}_k$ with $l$ units of discrete torsion (fractional M2-branes),
exist as unitary SCFTs only for $l \le k$, and $U(N+l)_k\times U(N)_{-k}$ is equivalent to
$U(N)_k\times U(N+k-l)_{-k}$. With gauge group $SU(2)\times SU(2)$ the same construction
gives the $\mathcal{N}=8$ BLG theory.

### Exact results from localization
Supersymmetric localization reduces $Z_{S^3}$ to a matrix model. Its planar limit gives
$F \propto N^{3/2}$ at strong coupling, the scaling of the number of degrees of freedom
on $N$ M2-branes, with the coefficient of the classical supergravity action [@abjm-3d/drukker2011]. At fixed $k$, all perturbative $1/N$ corrections sum to an Airy
function [@abjm-3d/fuji2011], which Mariño and Putrov [@abjm-3d/marino2012] derived by rewriting the
matrix model as an ideal Fermi gas.

The $\mathcal{N}=8$ numerical bootstrap bounds the CFT data as a function of $c_T$.
Comparing these bounds with BPS OPE coefficients computed by localization, Agmon,
Chester and Pufu [@abjm-3d/agmon2018] conjectured that some of the $\mathcal{N}=8$ ABJ(M) theories saturate
them (an OPE coefficient minimization principle).

theories.name: 3d BLG theory, $SU(2)_k \times SU(2)_{-k}$
theories.summary: $\mathcal{N}=8$ Chern–Simons-matter SCFTs with gauge group $SU(2)\times SU(2)$ (or its $\mathbb{Z}_2$ quotient) at levels $(k,-k)$, for every integer $k$. For $k \le 4$ they are dual to ABJ(M) theories or their interacting sectors.
theories.description:
Bagger and Lambert [@blg-3d/bagger2007; @blg-3d/bagger2008a; @blg-3d/bagger2008b], and Gustavsson [@blg-3d/gustavsson2009], constructed a theory of eight scalars
and their fermionic partners, valued in an algebra with a totally antisymmetric triple
product (a 3-algebra) and coupled to a non-dynamical gauge field, as a candidate
worldvolume theory of several M2-branes. It has 16 supercharges, conformal invariance and
an $SO(8)$ R-symmetry acting on the eight transverse scalars, and the Chern–Simons
coefficient is quantized. For the explicit example, the $\mathcal{A}_4$ 3-algebra with
gauge group $SO(4)$, Van Raamsdonk [@blg-3d/vanraamsdonk2008] rewrote the theory as an ordinary
$SU(2)\times SU(2)$ Chern–Simons theory with bifundamental matter, which clarifies its
parity invariance. In $\mathcal{N}=2$ language it is the ABJM quiver with
$SU(2)$ gauge factors: ABJM [@blg-3d/abjm2008] noted that their construction with gauge group
$SU(2)\times SU(2)$ has extra symmetry and coincides with the Bagger–Lambert theory.

There are two global forms, $SU(2)_k\times SU(2)_{-k}$ and
$(SU(2)_k\times SU(2)_{-k})/\mathbb{Z}_2$. Both have manifest $\mathcal{N}=8$
supersymmetry for every integer $k$, and they have the same stress-tensor four-point
function, so the $c_T$ values below apply to both [@blg-3d/agmon2018, fn. 4]. As
$k \to \infty$ the theory becomes weakly coupled and $c_T \to 64$, the value for its
free field content.

Lambert and Tong [@blg-3d/lambert2008] argued that the theory describes two membranes in the orbifold
$\mathbb{R}^8/\mathbb{Z}_2$; at $k = 1$ and $k = 2$ its classical moduli space coincides
with the infrared moduli space of $SO(4)$ and $SO(5)$ super Yang–Mills theory. Distler, Mukhi, Papageorgakis and Van Raamsdonk [@blg-3d/distler2008] argued that the moduli space at
level $k$ is $(\mathbb{R}^8\times\mathbb{R}^8)/D_{2k}$, with $D_{2k}$ the dihedral group of
order $4k$, and conjectured that the theory describes two M2-branes on a
$\mathbb{Z}_{2k}$ "M-fold". For general $k$ no M-theory interpretation is known.

### Dualities with ABJ(M) theories
In the notation $\mathrm{BLG}_k = (SU(2)_k\times SU(2)_{-k})/\mathbb{Z}_2$ and
$\mathrm{BLG}'_k = SU(2)_k\times SU(2)_{-k}$, the dualities listed by Agmon, Chester and
Pufu [@blg-3d/agmon2018b, Eqs. (2)–(3)] are:
- $\mathrm{BLG}_1$ $\cong$ $U(2)_1\times U(2)_{-1}$ ABJM, two M2-branes in flat space;
- $\mathrm{BLG}'_2$ $\cong$ $U(2)_2\times U(2)_{-2}$ ABJM;
- $\mathrm{BLG}_3$ $\otimes$ (free $\mathcal{N}=8$ theory) $\cong$ $U(3)_1\times U(3)_{-1}$ ABJM, so
  $\mathrm{BLG}_3$ is the interacting sector of three M2-branes in flat space;
- $\mathrm{BLG}_4$ $\cong$ $U(2)_2\times U(3)_{-2}$ ABJ.

Lambert and Papageorgakis [@blg-3d/lambert2010] derived the first by integrating out the $U(1)$ gauge field of
ABJM, and conjectured the second. Bashkirov and Kapustin [@blg-3d/bashkirov2011b] tested such dualities by
comparing superconformal indices. Agmon, Chester and Pufu [@blg-3d/agmon2018b] proposed the third and
supported it by matching moduli spaces, superconformal indices, $S^3$ partition functions
and BPS OPE coefficients. They also computed [@blg-3d/agmon2018, Secs. 3.3.1, 4] the BPS OPE coefficients of $\mathrm{BLG}_k$ for all
$k$ and found that, unlike some ABJ(M) theories, these generically do not saturate the
numerical bootstrap bounds.
